title: Guanyin's chapter chanted (Kern ch. 24)
hook: this chapter is chanted alone across East Asia
tomorrow: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the universal gate: Avalokiteshvara, who hears every cry and comes in the form that's needed. Your line: the one who hears. Did you catch a small cry and stop for it? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

On a temple bench, or at a small shrine on top of a kitchen cabinet, a few people sit with a thin booklet open and chant together. The booklet isn't the whole Lotus Sutra. It's one chapter, yesterday's, traveling on its own. The universal gate has had a life apart from the long book it came from, and in Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism it is recited as a short scripture of its own. So this time we stay with yesterday's chapter, and listen to how it is used. Today: Guanyin's chapter chanted.
screen: `A THIN BOOKLET ON A BENCH.` → `ONE CHAPTER, TRAVELING ALONE.` → `HOW IT IS USED.`

segments.voice: First, a chapter that became a book. Printed and chanted on its own, it is often called the Guanyin Sutra in Chinese, and in Japanese the Kannon-gyo. People recite it at home, in temples, in times of illness and fear, and on ordinary mornings. Second, the names. Guanyin is the Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara. The fuller form, Guanshiyin, is the name in Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus, and it is usually rendered: the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In Japan the name is Kannon, in Korea Gwaneum, in Vietnam Quan Am. And here yesterday's many forms come back. In Indian art the bodhisattva appears as a princely male figure. In Chinese art Guanyin is often shown as a woman in white robes. Some Buddhists in these traditions say the same compassion takes whatever form people can receive. Third, the verses. The chapter closes with verses that retell its promises in rhythm, easy to carry in the mouth. In them, someone pushed into a pit of fire calls the name, and the fire becomes a pool. Someone pushed off a mountain stays in the air, like the sun. The verses are full of falling and being held. Fourth, chanting as listening. The chapter is about a bodhisattva who hears. The people who chant it are calling out, and they are also practicing hearing: the sound in the room, the voices beside them, their own breath between lines. Some who chant it describe this as being heard and learning to hear, in the same breath.
screen: `A CHAPTER THAT BECAME A BOOK.` · `GUANYIN, KANNON, GWANEUM, QUAN AM.` · `VERSES OF FALLING AND BEING HELD.` · `CHANTING AS LISTENING.` · then, large: `CHANTED EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: chant a few lines. If you chant, you can say Guanyin's name the way it is said in Chinese temples, Namo Guanshiyin Pusa, slowly, once on each out-breath. If you'd rather not chant a name, hum one long, low note on each out-breath instead. Either way, the sound is half the practice. The other half is listening as it fades, all the way to silence, before the next breath. Stay with that rhythm. The bell holds the time.
Guanyin's chapter chanted. The universal gate chapter of the Lotus Sutra, recited on its own as a short scripture about the one who hears the world's cries. Today's word.

Your line: chanted everywhere. Today, notice one sound that repeats around you, a chime, a bell, a tune someone hums, and let it remind you of the one who hears. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 1181 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KING AND HIS SONS (KERN CH. 25).`

howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism, the universal gate chapter is recited on its own as a short scripture, and people call on Guanyin with the chant Namo Guanshiyin Pusa.

fork.setup: in the chapter's verses, someone is pushed into a pit of fire and calls the name of the one who hears. what happens?
options: the fire burns on, and they endure it
the fire is never mentioned again
fork.reveal: the verses say the fire pit turns into a pool; the whole poem is full of falling and being held.

original.note: Chinese: Guanshiyin, shortened to Guanyin; the name in Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus for Avalokiteshvara.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guanyin is a goddess from a different story than the Lotus Sutra.
what it means: Guanyin is Avalokiteshvara, and the Lotus chapter on the universal gate is chanted on its own as a scripture of its own.

what a scholar hears: Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus names the bodhisattva Guanshiyin, perceiver of the world's sounds; the chapter circulated separately as the Guanyin Sutra, and the figure's form changed as it traveled.

sources.ref: Saddharmapundarika, ch. 24 (Kern numbering; ch. 25 in Kumarajiva's Chinese), verses

notes: Paraphrased; nothing quoted. The verse images (fire pit becoming a pool; pushed from a mountain and staying in the air like the sun) are as found in the Chinese verses; confirm they are in Kern's Sanskrit verses too, or note the source.
The index says the chapter is 'chanted alone across East Asia'; the script names Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism and avoids numbers. Keeper to confirm.
Names: Guanshiyin (Kumarajiva), Kannon, Gwaneum, Quan Am (diacritics dropped in voice: Quan Âm). 'Perceives the sounds of the world' framed as 'usually rendered'.
Art history line (princely male in Indian art; often female in white in Chinese art) kept general; confirm.
Practice cites the devotional chant Namo Guanshiyin Pusa; this is a real chant, not a new prayer. Confirm wording.
Original: 觀世音 in traditional characters; the 'say' line gives plain syllables, not tones.
Editor: softened "Buddhists in these traditions say" to "some Buddhists"; removed a doubled "today" in the hook; fixed "a short scripture to" in the word line.
